Elon Musk just made a Tesla fly, sort of. The new Roadster flipped over a row of cars on SpaceX's thrusters, and it may have been more than a car demo. It may have been a preview of Tesla and SpaceX becoming one company.

Musk has written that idea off in the past. But more recently, he's said himself that his companies are "trending towards convergence." Since then, the speculation hasn't stopped. Barclays now expects SpaceX to buy Tesla, possibly within months. So what changed his mind? And what would they even look like put together?

The answer starts with the car itself. Because on paper, it's a Tesla. But it couldn't have gotten off the ground without SpaceX.

## An Engineering Flex

It hung upside down under a ramp, dropped off and rolled in midair. Then it cleared a row of Teslas, a Semi among them.

And look at where they did it. Not at a Tesla factory, but at SpaceX's rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, with SpaceX's thrusters bolted onto a Tesla. Before the first stunt, Musk told the crowd exactly what they were about to see.

<Quote collection="tesla-spacex" figure="clue_roadster_musk_collaboration_remark_oct2026" />

The Verge called it "completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold."

And that was exactly the point. It was a joint demonstration. An opportunity for Elon to flex Tesla and SpaceX's engineering prowess and provide a taste of what the two companies could build together.

But Elon didn't always think the companies were a fit.

## Musk Changed His Tune

Back in 2016, Musk said there was no "strong product rationale to combine SpaceX and Tesla." But last year, he posted that "my companies are, surprisingly in some ways, trending towards convergence." He's even begun shutting down the question on analyst calls, stating that "we can't talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It's got to be done with the appropriate process."

The press has been circling the topic all year. Bloomberg and CNBC both reported Musk had weighed folding the two together. JPMorgan called it "strategically coherent on paper." Even SpaceX's president said a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier."

And people are betting real money on it. By the morning after the Roadster, the odds of a deal by March had jumped from 29% to 56%, then cooled to 45% a day later.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-tune-changes" />

Nonetheless, the companies continue to become more intertwined. Tesla invested $2 billion into xAI. SpaceX buys Tesla's Megapack batteries for its AI data centers. Grok is in Tesla's cars. And the two companies have also said they plan to build a chip factory together.

And the biggest clue is SpaceX itself. This year it bought xAI, and with it Grok and X. It went public at about $1.8 trillion and is currently worth more than Tesla. And it's already spent $60 billion in stock this year to buy Cursor. So if you're curious how Elon might structure the deal, there's a lot of precedent to work off of. And Tesla is the last big piece.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-last-big-piece" />

## The Deal on the Table

So what if they combined? What if Tesla's factories and SpaceX's technology were one company?

Barclays thinks it would look like this. In a note last week, its analyst wrote that he expects SpaceX to buy Tesla in a stock-for-stock deal, which means Tesla's shareholders would get SpaceX shares instead of cash. SpaceX is now the more valuable of the two. At the close on October 16th, it was worth about $1.98 trillion and Tesla about $1.4 trillion, so each Tesla share was worth about 2.43 SpaceX shares, before the premium Barclays expects Tesla's holders to get. Together, that's a company worth about $3.4 trillion.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-deal-on-the-table" />

And one man would have voting control of the whole thing.

But to understand what it would cost and who'd be in charge, you first have to understand what the two would actually do better together.

## Where It Clicks

Tesla is still primarily a car company. It brought in about $95 billion of revenue last year, and about three quarters of that came from its car business. What it's best at is building complicated hardware at enormous scale. Last quarter alone, it delivered more than 486,000 cars. But it also has a fast-growing energy business, selling the giant Megapack batteries that back up power grids, and increasingly, AI data centers.

But investors aren't paying $1.4 trillion for the cars. Tesla's value is a bet on autonomy, in two parts. The first is self-driving. About 1.5 million people already pay for Tesla's self-driving software, and Tesla now runs robotaxis with nobody behind the wheel in six cities. It's still small, with only a few million dollars of fares so far by our estimate, but Tesla has built a line in Texas to make more than 125,000 Cybercabs a year, a car designed from the start to be a robotaxi. The second bet is Optimus, Tesla's humanoid robot. They aren't on sale yet, and the newest version hasn't even been shown, but Tesla is planning for a million robots a year, and Musk has said about 80% of Tesla's value will be Optimus.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-autonomy-bet" />

SpaceX is a more layered business. Shaun Maguire, the Sequoia partner who runs its investments in SpaceX, told Bloomberg he thinks of it in five layers.

Layer one is launch, the foundation. SpaceX flew 170 missions last year, and it says it carried more than 80% of everything the world sent to orbit. If you need to put something big into space, there's essentially one call to make. And Starship, its rocket built to be fully reusable and to carry 100 tons at a time, put its first satellites into orbit last month.

Layer two is connectivity: Starlink, and now service straight to phones. About 9,600 satellites and 12 million subscribers, double a year ago, and on our math from SpaceX's own figures, margins of around 60% before it spends on growth. This is the proven layer, the cash engine of the whole company.

Layer three is compute. SpaceX is now a hyperscaler, which basically means a company that rents out computing power, the way Amazon and Microsoft do. It has about 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing, Google rents capacity from it, and Anthropic alone has agreed to pay it a massive $1.25 billion a month. It's almost all on the ground today, but SpaceX wants to put data centers in orbit, with its first AI satellites planned for 2027.

Layer four is the models and the apps that run on them: Grok, X, and now Cursor. And in Maguire's words, "most investors don't know how to assess where SpaceX, SpaceX AI is today."

And layer five is "all the other bets": Terafab, the chip factory it's planning with Tesla, and someday, a base on the Moon.

And the money is moving up the layers fast. Last year, Starlink was about 60% of SpaceX's revenue, launch about a fifth, and AI less than that. By the second quarter, AI was already a third of SpaceX's $7.8 billion of revenue, and launch was down to about an eighth.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-five-layers" />

And this is where it gets really interesting. Step back, and look at what each one has. SpaceX already has launch, satellites, data centers and AI. Tesla has power, manufacturing at scale, robotics and autonomy. And all of these make each other better.

You can already see it. Tesla's batteries help power SpaceX's AI. SpaceX's Starlink is going into the Cybercab. Grok is already in Tesla's cars, and Musk wants it all running Optimus.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-loop" />

Add in their bigger bets, computers in orbit and humanoid robots, and it starts to look like an unstoppable force.

And if they consolidate into one company, the scale of the business makes life a lot easier too.

## One Balance Sheet

So let's look at the numbers, starting with each company on its own. Tesla brought in about $95 billion of revenue last year. That's still enormous, but the profits have gotten thin. In the second quarter, its operating income was under $400 million, and most of what it earned on paper came from the rising value of its SpaceX shares. And it plans to spend more than $25 billion this year building what comes next.

SpaceX is smaller, but growing much faster. It made about $19 billion last year, and $7.8 billion in the second quarter alone, up 92% from a year earlier. It's still losing a little money, because it's pouring cash into the build: about $18 billion of capex in a single quarter, most of it on AI. But it's sitting on about $100 billion of cash, mostly from its IPO.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="each-on-its-own" />

Put them together, and you get a company that brought in about $114 billion of revenue last year, holds about $144 billion of cash, and is worth about $3.4 trillion. That's one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="one-balance-sheet" />

And yes, that's a premium price. $3.4 trillion is about 30 times what the two made last year, and SpaceX alone is valued at about a hundred times its revenue. Investors aren't paying for today's business. They're paying for the most comprehensive set of bets on the market. These two are already at the front of some of the biggest markets there are: autonomous driving, space, AI and computing. And they're positioning for the frontier ones that barely exist yet, like data centers in orbit and humanoid robots.

Musk, of course, thinks a lot bigger. On SpaceX's first earnings call, he said the company's "internal projections for reaching a trillion dollars in revenue" had "moved up from 2031 to 2030." Last year, he wrote that about 80% of Tesla's value will be Optimus. And on October 14th, the night before the Roadster event, replying to a post about investor Ron Baron's forecast of $20 to $50 trillion, he wrote, "Unless there is a major world war, SpaceX probably gets to" more than $100 trillion in less than 10 years.

I'm not underwriting that $100 trillion number, or giving you a view on it. Getting from about $2 trillion today to $100 trillion in ten years would take some serious growth, roughly 48% a year, every year, for a decade. But if any company has the potential to even fathom it, it's this one.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="a-hundred-trillion" />

So the price is a bet on Musk being right about the future. And if the two combine, he'd be the one in charge of getting there.

## Where It Lands

But a deal this big comes with strings, and the first one is control. Musk owns about a fifth of Tesla. At SpaceX, he controls more than 80% of the votes, through special Class B shares that carry ten votes each. So if Tesla's stock were swapped into SpaceX's, Musk would end up with voting control of the whole combined company. Barclays puts it at more than half the votes. And Musk has been clear that this matters to him: "I don't feel comfortable wielding that robot army if I don't have at least a strong influence."

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="control" />

Then there are the regulators. A deal like this needs antitrust review, and it wouldn't be a normal one. About a fifth of SpaceX's revenue comes from the U.S. government, so national security would be on the table, and JPMorgan sees a "practical bottleneck" in getting approvals in China. And Tesla's shareholders have been here before. When Tesla bought SolarCity, another Musk company, a court later said Musk "should have stepped away" from the board's review. This deal would be more than 600 times bigger.

So when could it happen? Both companies report earnings this month, SpaceX on October 20th and Tesla the next day. But don't expect a deal on an earnings call. Musk has said himself it has to go through "the appropriate process," and the betting markets give it about a 4% chance before November. The date to watch is Tesla's annual shareholder meeting, due by December 6th. Barclays thinks that could be the moment: announce a deal in time, and Tesla's shareholders could vote on it right there. If not, Barclays sees six to twelve months.

Ten years ago, Musk said there was no strong reason to put SpaceX and Tesla together. Now he's spent a night showing us one. The only question left is whether he makes it official.
